issues.legal_issue: A High Court hearing a second appeal cannot reverse concurrent factual findings by reappraising evidence unless the findings are perverse.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court found that the disputed properties had been acquired separately and were not joint family properties.
The properties had been acquired before the family partition and were excluded from the registered partition, which allotted other properties to the family member concerned.
The High Court reappraised the evidence and reversed the concurrent findings without those findings being shown to rest on a misreading of evidence or on no evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure by reversing the concurrent findings; the lower courts’ findings were correct and the High Court’s reversal could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal lies only where a substantial question of law is involved. The High Court cannot reappraise evidence to set aside factual findings unless the first appellate court’s findings are perverse, such as being based on misreading of evidence or on no evidence. The Court relied on Kshitish Chandra Purkait v. Santosh Kumar Purkait, Panchugopal Barua v. Umesh Chandra Goswami, Kondiba Dagadu Kadam v. Savitribai Sopan Gujar, Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari, Thiagarajan v. Sri Venugopalaswamay B. Koil, and Govindaraju v. Mariamman.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and assets_excluded_from_partition and not finding_perverse

predicates.second_appeal: The case is an appeal to a High Court from a decree passed in appeal by a subordinate court.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual finding about the properties.
predicates.assets_excluded_from_partition: The properties at issue were omitted from a family partition that dealt with other family properties.
predicates.finding_perverse: The factual finding was based on a misreading of evidence or on no evidence.

issues.definition: When a second appeal concerns concurrent factual findings, the properties were excluded from the partition, and the findings were not perverse, the High Court cannot reverse those findings.

issues.legal_issue: In a second appeal, a High Court cannot decide the validity or genuineness of a deed or will on an issue that was not challenged by the parties or framed as a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court found that the settlement deed and will had been duly executed and were genuine.
The respondents did not challenge the deeds’ genuineness or due execution in their pleadings, evidence, or grounds of second appeal.

The High Court framed a substantial question concerning whether certain properties were joint family properties, but did not frame an additional question concerning the deeds’ validity or genuineness.
issues.conclusion: The High Court lacked jurisdiction to set aside the lower courts’ findings about the settlement deed and will; its findings on those matters were vitiated and could not be sustained.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100(3)–(5) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires a second appeal to be heard on the substantial questions of law formulated by the High Court. The proviso to Section 100(5) permits hearing an additional substantial question only if the High Court is satisfied that it arises and records reasons for that satisfaction. Under Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari, the High Court may hear an additional question only on those conditions.

predicates.second_appeal: The case is an appeal to a High Court from a decree passed in appeal by a subordinate court.
predicates.issue_not_challenged_by_parties: The parties did not dispute the issue in their pleadings, evidence, or grounds of appeal.
predicates.no_substantial_question_framed_for_issue: The High Court did not formulate a substantial question of law addressing the issue.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, if the parties did not challenge an issue and the High Court did not frame a substantial question of law about it, the High Court cannot decide that issue.
